snippets.title: Spark plug inspection and gap check
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines. Remove the spark plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with a plug from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in) and look for a cracked insulator, carbon tracking down the porcelain, or oil or fuel fouling.

snippets.title: Rotor lateral runout measurement
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles with front disc brakes. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the steering knuckle and set the plunger about 0.5 in from the outer edge of the rotor face. Rotate the rotor one full turn. Lateral runout must not exceed 0.002 in.

snippets.title: Harsh 1-2 upshift on a cold transmission
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2014-2020. A harsh 1-2 upshift may occur only during the first few minutes of driving below 40 deg F and stop once the transmission warms. Review the transmission fluid temperature reading during the event. Repair: update the transmission control software.

snippets.title: Battery lamp at cold startup with belt squeal
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles with a belt-driven alternator. Below 10 deg F, the battery warning lamp may light for the first minute after a cold start with a short belt squeal, and it clears once the engine warms. Inspect the belt for contamination and check the tensioner damping. Repair: install the revised tensioner.

messages.content: Customer vehicle: 2016 compact sedan, 1.8L, 107,834 mi. The brake pedal pulses and the steering wheel shakes when I brake from highway speed on dry pavement. It's smooth when I'm not braking.

snippets.title: Fuel pressure and hold test, returnless systems
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines with a fuel rail test port. Key on, engine off, connect a pressure gauge at the rail test port. Specified pressure is 55-62 psi, and it should hold within 5 psi for 5 minutes after key-off. Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.

snippets.title: Intake vacuum leak smoke test
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines. With the engine off, introduce smoke into the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the intake manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke. A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

snippets.title: Extended crank on cold mornings from fuel pump check valve
snippets.text: Applies to 1.8L I4 and 2.0L I4 engines, model years 2010-2016. A long crank may occur only after the vehicle sits overnight below 40 deg F; restarts with a warm engine are normal. Leave a gauge on the rail test port overnight and compare the morning reading with the reading at shutdown. Repair: replace the fuel pump module.

snippets.title: Lean code at idle from cracked PCV hose
snippets.text: Applies to 2.0L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2012-2020. Some vehicles may set P0171 (system too lean, bank 1) with a rough idle that is worst on a cold engine. The PCV hose can crack on its underside where it joins the intake elbow, admitting unmetered air. With the engine idling, inspect the hose at the elbow and flex it gently while listening for a vacuum hiss. Repair: replace the PCV hose and clamp.

messages.content: Working on a 2013 midsize sedan (2.5L four-cylinder, 108k miles). CEL came on with P0171. It idles rough at stoplights and stumbles a little right after a cold start, but it pulls fine on the highway. What should I check first?
With the engine idling, inspect the PCV hose where it joins the intake elbow, flexing it gently while you listen for a vacuum hiss [SB 28-660]. That result will show whether this area is involved.
Is that really necessary? I was going to put a new fuel pump in anyway.
I'd hold off on buying anything until this is checked. With the engine idling, inspect the PCV hose where it joins the intake elbow, flexing it gently while you listen for a vacuum hiss [SB 28-660].
Alright, ran that check. I flexed the PCV hose at the elbow with it idling. No cracks and no hiss.

Good, that looks normal. With the engine off, smoke-test the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke [SM-0707].
A shop smoke-tested the intake for me. No smoke came out anywhere. I'm done testing. What do I replace?

snippets.title: Spark plug inspection and gap check
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines. Remove the spark plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with a plug from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in) and look for a cracked insulator, carbon tracking down the porcelain, or oil or fuel fouling.

snippets.title: Internal coolant loss at intake manifold gasket
snippets.text: Applies to 3.4L V6 engines, model years 2020-2022. Coolant loss with no external leak may come from the intake manifold gasket at a coolant passage. Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the gasket area with a borescope through the throttle body opening. Repair: replace the intake manifold gaskets.

snippets.title: Brake vibration while towing
snippets.text: Applies to full-size pickups with the 5.5L V8, model years 2021-2023. A brake vibration may occur only during stops while towing a trailer over 5,000 lb. Check trailer brake gain settings and inspect rotors for heat spots. Repair: install revised front rotors.

messages.content: I have a 2011 midsize SUV with the 3.4-liter V6, about 71k miles. The coolant level drops slowly between oil changes. I can't see any leak, there's no sweet smell inside, and it never runs hot. Unrelated maybe, but the check engine light flashes when I accelerate hard or climb hills, and it stored P0303 (cylinder 3 misfire). Idle is smooth, and it does it in dry weather too. I already have a new water pump sitting in my garage. Should I just install it?

snippets.title: LED headlamp flicker from lamp driver software
snippets.text: Applies to midsize SUVs with LED headlamps, model years 2020-2022. Headlamps may flicker at idle while charging voltage is normal and no battery warning appears. Check the lamp driver module for stored codes. Repair: update the lamp driver module software.

snippets.title: Low state of charge on short trips with auto start-stop
snippets.text: Applies to 1.4L turbo I4 engines with auto start-stop, model years 2019-2021. Vehicles driven mostly on trips under 10 minutes may show a low battery message because the battery monitoring sensor limits charging. Check the battery monitoring sensor data with a scan tool. Repair: update the body control software and reset the sensor.

messages.content: If the car sits for two or three days, the battery is dead. It starts fine with a jump and drives normally, and the weather has been mild. Working on a 2015 midsize sedan (3.5L V6, 118k miles). What's the first thing to look at?

snippets.title: Alternator AC ripple test
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Higher ripple indicates a failed diode in the alternator rectifier, which reduces output and can cause lights to flicker.

snippets.title: Misfire in wet weather from coil boot tracking
snippets.text: Applies to 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2013-2019. A misfire may occur at idle or light throttle only during rain or after a car wash, and it clears once the engine bay dries. Mist water over the coils with the engine idling and watch for arcing at the coil boots in a dark shop. Repair: install updated coil boots and apply dielectric grease.

snippets.title: Harsh 1-2 upshift on a cold transmission
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2014-2020. A harsh 1-2 upshift may occur only during the first few minutes of driving below 40 deg F and stop once the transmission warms. Review the transmission fluid temperature reading during the event. Repair: update the transmission control software.

messages.content: My midsize SUV is a 2018 with the 3.4-liter V6 and 187k on the clock. Upshifts are harsh, especially 2-3, and there's a delay before it engages. It gets worse the longer I drive. There's another problem too. At stoplights at night the headlights and dash lights pulse dim and bright, and the battery warning light flickers, even on warm evenings. It's fine once I'm moving. The cup holder lid won't stay closed. Where should I begin with this?

snippets.title: Condenser fan operation with AC on
snippets.text: Applies to all models with an electric condenser fan. With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises and vent air warms up in traffic.

snippets.title: Intake vacuum leak smoke test
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines. With the engine off, introduce smoke into the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the intake manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke. A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

snippets.title: Low-speed pulsation felt in the seat from rear drums
snippets.text: Applies to hatchbacks with rear drum brakes, model years 2012-2015. A pulsation felt through the seat, not the steering wheel, may occur during light stops below 25 mph from out-of-round rear drums. Measure rear drum diameter at several points. Repair: replace the rear drums.

snippets.title: Compressor clutch engagement check
snippets.text: Applies to all models with a clutch-driven compressor. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.

messages.content: My full-size pickup is a 2020 with the 5.5L V8 and 87,964 on the clock. P0171 keeps coming back a day after I clear it. The idle shakes the steering wheel a bit when it's cold, and the freeze frame says it set at idle. What's the best first check?

snippets.title: Combustion leak (block) test
snippets.text: Applies to all engines. With the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself.

snippets.title: Coolant expelled from reservoir after overheating
snippets.text: Applies to 3.5L V6, 3.4L V6 and 5.5L V8 engines, model years 2011-2021. Coolant loss that appears only after the temperature gauge has climbed past normal during towing or mountain driving is usually coolant pushed out through the overflow. Check the overflow hose routing and the reservoir vent for kinks. Repair: install the revised reservoir cap and vent hose.

messages.content: Working on a 2015 compact sedan (2.0-liter four, 144k miles). I have to top off the coolant reservoir every week or two. There are no puddles under the car and it has never overheated. What would you look at first?

snippets.title: Rear clunk over bumps from leaf spring shackles
snippets.text: Applies to full-size pickups, model years 2013-2020. A clunk from the rear of the truck over bumps may come from dry leaf spring shackle bushings. Inspect the rear shackles for play with the truck on the ground. Repair: replace the shackle bushings.

snippets.title: Clicking or clunk at full steering lock
snippets.text: Applies to all front-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive vehicles. A clicking or clunking noise that occurs only when turning sharply at full lock, such as in parking lots, may come from a worn outer CV joint. Inspect the outer CV boots for tears and grease loss. Repair: replace the axle shaft.

messages.content: I need a straight answer, not a diagnostic flowchart. The front left side knocks over bumps, even small ones, driving straight at low speed. Turning at full lock is quiet. My midsize sedan is a 2013 with the 3.5L V6 and 113,610 on the clock. I already have a new sway bar link sitting in my garage. Should I just install it?

snippets.title: Slow cranking on a hot engine
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. If the engine turns over noticeably slower when hot than when cold, measure starter current draw with an inductive clamp while cranking with fuel disabled. Draw above 250 A on a four- or six-cylinder engine indicates excessive starter load. This procedure covers slow crank speed only, not an engine that cranks at normal speed but is slow to fire.

snippets.title: Charging circuit voltage drop test
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. With the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy electrical loads on, measure voltage drop from the alternator output terminal to the battery positive post, and from the alternator case to the battery negative post. Drop should be under 0.3 V on the positive side and under 0.2 V on the ground side.

snippets.title: Rotor lateral runout measurement
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles with front disc brakes. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the steering knuckle and set the plunger about 0.5 in from the outer edge of the rotor face. Rotate the rotor one full turn. Lateral runout must not exceed 0.002 in.

messages.content: I need a straight answer, not a diagnostic flowchart. Pedal pulsation when slowing down from highway speed, felt mostly through the steering wheel rather than the seat. No vibration while cruising, and I'm not towing anything. It's a 2011 midsize SUV, 3.4-liter V6, roughly 80,916 miles. Is it the front rotor? A simple yes or no is fine.

snippets.title: Rotor thickness variation
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles with front disc brakes. Using an outside micrometer, measure rotor thickness at eight evenly spaced points about 0.5 in from the outer edge. Thickness variation must not exceed 0.0005 in. Variation above this limit produces pedal pulsation during braking from speed.

snippets.title: Rotor surface inspection for uneven pad transfer
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles with front disc brakes. Remove the front wheels and inspect both faces of each rotor in good light. Dark, blotchy patches of pad material, or blue-gray hard spots that a file skates over, indicate uneven pad transfer or hard spots that grab the pad once per revolution and are felt as pulsation when braking from speed.

snippets.title: Pedal pulsation at low speed on rough roads from ABS activation
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles with ABS. A pedal pulsation with a buzzing sound may occur during stops below 15 mph on gravel or broken pavement because of early ABS activation. Inspect the wheel speed sensor tone rings for rust jacking. Repair: replace the affected hub and tone ring.

messages.content: Customer vehicle: 2020 full-size pickup, 5.5L V8, 56,775 mi. The brake pedal pulses and the steering wheel shakes when I brake from highway speed on dry pavement. It's smooth when I'm not braking. Where should I begin with this?

With the front wheels off, inspect both faces of each front rotor in good light for dark patches of pad material or blue-gray hard spots [SM 2.7.5]. That result will show whether this area is involved.
Done. Both rotors have a uniform finish on both faces, nothing blotchy.
That rules that area out. Measure front rotor thickness with a micrometer at eight evenly spaced points about half an inch from the edge; variation should be under 0.0005 in [SM 2.7.7].
Thickness variation was 0.0003 inch on both rotors. I'm done testing. What do I replace?

snippets.title: Hot restart delay from fuel pump relay contacts
snippets.text: Applies to 5.5L V8 engines, model years 2021-2023. After towing or extended idling in hot weather, worn contacts in the fuel pump relay can delay fuel pump prime on restart. Check the relay terminals for discoloration and record fuel pressure during the first crank. Repair: replace the fuel pump relay.

snippets.title: Intake vacuum leak smoke test
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines. With the engine off, introduce smoke into the intake through the brake booster vacuum line and watch the intake manifold gasket, throttle body gasket, PCV hoses and vacuum lines for escaping smoke. A lean code that is worst at idle and improves above 2,000 rpm usually indicates unmetered air entering after the airflow sensor.

snippets.title: Mass airflow sensor reading at idle
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines with a mass airflow sensor. With the engine at operating temperature and idling with all accessories off, read MAF airflow on a scan tool. Expect roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement (about 2-2.5 g/s for a 2.0L engine). A reading well below that while long-term fuel trim is high suggests the sensor is under-reporting airflow.

messages.content: 2015 minivan, 3.5-liter V6, 158,171 miles. It starts right up cold, but if I shut it off warm and come back 20 minutes later it cranks a long time before starting. The starter spins at its usual speed. Is it the coolant temperature sensor? A simple yes or no is fine.

snippets.title: Internal coolant loss at intake manifold gasket
snippets.text: Applies to 3.4L V6 engines, model years 2020-2022. Coolant loss with no external leak may come from the intake manifold gasket at a coolant passage. Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the gasket area with a borescope through the throttle body opening. Repair: replace the intake manifold gaskets.

snippets.title: Coolant expelled from reservoir after overheating
snippets.text: Applies to 3.5L V6, 3.4L V6 and 5.5L V8 engines, model years 2011-2021. Coolant loss that appears only after the temperature gauge has climbed past normal during towing or mountain driving is usually coolant pushed out through the overflow. Check the overflow hose routing and the reservoir vent for kinks. Repair: install the revised reservoir cap and vent hose.

snippets.title: Coolant seepage at turbocharger coolant line
snippets.text: Applies to 1.4L turbo I4 engines, model years 2016-2018. Slow coolant loss may come from a seeping turbocharger coolant return line fitting. Inspect the fitting and the line for dried coolant residue with the engine cold. Repair: replace the coolant line and sealing washers.

messages.content: My full-size pickup is a 2019 with the 5.5-liter V8 and 154k on the clock. The coolant level drops slowly between oil changes. I can't see any leak, there's no sweet smell inside, and it never runs hot. What should I check first?

snippets.title: Overheating at idle from slipping fan clutch
snippets.text: Applies to 5.5L V8 engines with an engine-driven fan, model years 2013-2020. Temperature may climb at idle and in slow traffic if the viscous fan clutch slips. With the engine off and cool, spin the fan by hand: it should turn no more than about one revolution. Repair: replace the fan clutch.

snippets.title: Temperature gauge reads high with normal coolant temperature
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans with the 2.0L I4 engine, model years 2020-2022. The temperature gauge may read high in traffic while actual coolant temperature is normal. Compare the gauge with the coolant temperature reading on a scan tool. Repair: update the instrument cluster software.

snippets.title: High coolant temperature at sustained highway speed
snippets.text: Applies to 3.5L V6 engines, model years 2011-2018. Coolant temperature may rise during sustained highway driving or towing while temperature in stop-and-go traffic stays normal. Inspect the lower radiator hose for collapse at high rpm with the engine warm. Repair: install the reinforced lower hose.

messages.content: Got stuck in a drive-through line and the temp gauge went almost to the red. Once I got back on the road it came down. It never runs hot at highway speed. Customer vehicle: 2014 compact sedan, 2.0L, 124,351 mi. Where do I start?

snippets.title: Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check
snippets.text: Applies to all engines. With the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.

snippets.title: Misfire in wet weather from coil boot tracking
snippets.text: Applies to 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2013-2019. A misfire may occur at idle or light throttle only during rain or after a car wash, and it clears once the engine bay dries. Mist water over the coils with the engine idling and watch for arcing at the coil boots in a dark shop. Repair: install updated coil boots and apply dielectric grease.

snippets.title: Clear-flood crank test for hot restart concerns
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines. On a hot restart, crank with the accelerator pedal held to the floor; the control module cuts injector pulse in this clear-flood mode. If the engine starts noticeably faster in clear-flood mode, it is being overfueled on hot restarts. If it cranks just as long, excess fuel is unlikely and fuel supply or spark should be examined.

messages.content: The check engine light flashes when I accelerate hard or climb hills, and it stored P0304 (cylinder 4 misfire). Idle is smooth, and it does it in dry weather too. I have a 2013 midsize sedan with the 3.5-liter V6, about 58k miles. What would you look at first?

snippets.title: Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check
snippets.text: Applies to all engines. With the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.

snippets.title: Slow cranking on a hot engine
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. If the engine turns over noticeably slower when hot than when cold, measure starter current draw with an inductive clamp while cranking with fuel disabled. Draw above 250 A on a four- or six-cylinder engine indicates excessive starter load. This procedure covers slow crank speed only, not an engine that cranks at normal speed but is slow to fire.

snippets.title: Residual fuel pressure after hot shutdown
snippets.text: Applies to all gasoline engines with a fuel rail test port. Drive until the engine is at full operating temperature, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and record the pressure 20 minutes later. Pressure should stay above 30 psi. A faster drop lets fuel boil in the hot rail, which shows up as a long crank on restarts after a short stop.

messages.content: 2016 compact crossover, 2.4L, 167k miles. Hot restarts are the problem. After a short stop at the store it cranks at normal speed but takes forever to catch. First start of the day is fine.

Start with this: with the engine fully warm, compare the coolant temperature reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading at the thermostat housing; they should agree within 10 deg F [SEC 1.2].
Honestly I think it's the fuel pump. Can I skip the test?

Naming a part now would be a guess. With the engine fully warm, compare the coolant temperature reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading at the thermostat housing; they should agree within 10 deg F [SEC 1.2].
OK, I tried it. Scan tool said 201 and the infrared gun said 196 at the housing.
Good, that looks normal. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the fuel rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later; it should still be above 30 psi [SM 1.7.5].
Put a gauge on after a drive. Still 42 psi after twenty minutes. What now?

snippets.title: Line pressure test
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission (not CVT or manual). Connect a pressure gauge to the line pressure test port. With the engine idling in drive and the brake applied, line pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. High line pressure produces harsh engagement; low pressure produces slipping and delayed shifts.

snippets.title: Electric radiator fan operation check
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with electric radiator fans (2.0L I4, 2.4L I4, 2.5L I4, 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 1.4L turbo I4, 3.5L V6 and 3.4L V6 engines; not the 5.5L V8). With the engine at operating temperature and idling, turn the AC on or command the radiator fan on with a scan tool. The fan should start within a few moments. A fan that does not run lets coolant temperature climb in traffic while highway airflow keeps it normal at speed.

snippets.title: Spark output test with an adjustable spark tester
snippets.text: Applies to all engines with individual coil-on-plug ignition. Remove the coil from the misfiring cylinder, connect an adjustable spark tester set to 25 kV between the coil and engine ground, and crank with fuel disabled. A strong blue spark should jump the gap on every crank. A weak, orange or intermittent spark indicates the coil cannot supply enough voltage under load.

messages.content: 2014 minivan, 3.5L V6, 96,303 miles. Got stuck in a drive-through line and the temp gauge went almost to the red. Once I got back on the road it came down. It never runs hot at highway speed. Where do I start?

snippets.title: Recharge check for repeat dead batteries
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. A battery that is not brought back to full charge during normal driving goes flat after a few days parked even with no excess draw. After a 20 minute drive, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights and blower on, measure voltage at the battery posts. A reading of 13.5-14.7 V shows the charging system is recharging the battery.

snippets.title: No-start in extreme cold
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. In temperatures below 0 deg F, a battery that is healthy in mild weather may not crank the engine after sitting overnight, with no parasitic draw present. Check the battery temperature rating and whether a block heater is fitted and used. Repair: install a higher CCA battery or a battery warmer.

snippets.title: Dead battery after parking from audio module staying awake
snippets.text: Applies to midsize sedans and compact crossovers, model years 2021-2023. The battery may go flat after the vehicle is parked for two to three days because the audio module fails to enter sleep mode. After the vehicle has been locked for 60 minutes, measure draw at the negative battery terminal and note whether it drops below 50 mA when the radio fuse is pulled. Repair: reprogram the audio module.

snippets.title: Misfire in wet weather from coil boot tracking
snippets.text: Applies to 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2013-2019. A misfire may occur at idle or light throttle only during rain or after a car wash, and it clears once the engine bay dries. Mist water over the coils with the engine idling and watch for arcing at the coil boots in a dark shop. Repair: install updated coil boots and apply dielectric grease.

messages.content: 2016 minivan, 3.5-liter V6, 118,794 miles. If the car sits for two or three days, the battery is dead. It starts fine with a jump and drives normally, and the weather has been mild. What should I check first?

snippets.title: Automatic transmission fluid level and condition
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission (not CVT or manual). With the fluid at operating temperature, the engine idling in park and the vehicle level, check the fluid level against the hot range. Fluid should be red or pink with no burnt odor or debris. Low or degraded fluid causes delayed and harsh shifts.

snippets.title: Warm air from passenger side only on dual-zone systems
snippets.text: Applies to all models with dual-zone automatic climate control. The driver side may blow cold while the passenger side blows warm because the passenger temperature door loses calibration. Run the climate control self-test and read stored HVAC codes. Repair: recalibrate the passenger temperature door actuator.

snippets.title: Compressor clutch engagement check
snippets.text: Applies to all models with a clutch-driven compressor. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.

messages.content: The AC blows warm from every front vent, driver and passenger side alike. It was cold last summer. The blower works on all speeds. Vehicle is a 2015 midsize sedan with the 3.5L V6. Odometer shows 49,110.

snippets.title: Temperature gauge reads high with normal coolant temperature
snippets.text: Applies to compact sedans with the 2.0L I4 engine, model years 2020-2022. The temperature gauge may read high in traffic while actual coolant temperature is normal. Compare the gauge with the coolant temperature reading on a scan tool. Repair: update the instrument cluster software.

snippets.title: Overheating at idle from slipping fan clutch
snippets.text: Applies to 5.5L V8 engines with an engine-driven fan, model years 2013-2020. Temperature may climb at idle and in slow traffic if the viscous fan clutch slips. With the engine off and cool, spin the fan by hand: it should turn no more than about one revolution. Repair: replace the fan clutch.

snippets.title: Radiator temperature drop check
snippets.text: Applies to all engines. With the engine at operating temperature and the thermostat open, use an infrared thermometer to compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical. A much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow through the radiator.

messages.content: It runs hot at idle. In stop-and-go traffic the gauge creeps up past the middle, but on the highway it stays right where it should. I have a 2017 compact crossover with the 2.4L four-cylinder, about 66k miles.

snippets.title: Charging circuit voltage drop test
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. With the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy electrical loads on, measure voltage drop from the alternator output terminal to the battery positive post, and from the alternator case to the battery negative post. Drop should be under 0.3 V on the positive side and under 0.2 V on the ground side.

snippets.title: Accessory drive belt and tensioner inspection
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles with a belt-driven alternator. With the engine off, inspect the accessory drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. A glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip at idle under electrical load.

snippets.title: Battery warning after auto start-stop restart
snippets.text: Applies to 1.4L turbo I4 engines with auto start-stop, model years 2019-2021. The battery warning lamp may flash briefly when the engine restarts after an auto stop. Review battery sensor data and stored body control codes. Repair: replace the battery monitoring sensor.

snippets.title: Alternator AC ripple test
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Higher ripple indicates a failed diode in the alternator rectifier, which reduces output and can cause lights to flicker.

snippets.title: Harsh 1-2 upshift on a cold transmission
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a conventional automatic transmission, model years 2014-2020. A harsh 1-2 upshift may occur only during the first few minutes of driving below 40 deg F and stop once the transmission warms. Review the transmission fluid temperature reading during the event. Repair: update the transmission control software.

Good, that looks normal. With the engine at 2,000 rpm and heavy loads on, measure voltage drop between the alternator output terminal and the battery positive post [SM 4.9.2].

snippets.title: Battery state-of-health test
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked.

snippets.title: CVT judder on light acceleration
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with a CVT, model years 2017-2022. A judder or shudder may be felt during light acceleration from 15-35 mph. Check CVT fluid condition and the transmission control software level. Repair: replace the CVT fluid and update the control software.

snippets.title: Battery warning after auto start-stop restart
snippets.text: Applies to 1.4L turbo I4 engines with auto start-stop, model years 2019-2021. The battery warning lamp may flash briefly when the engine restarts after an auto stop. Review battery sensor data and stored body control codes. Repair: replace the battery monitoring sensor.

snippets.title: Battery drain from infotainment head unit
snippets.text: Applies to full-size pickups with the 5.5L V8, model years 2021-2023. snippets.title: LED headlamp flicker from lamp driver software
snippets.text: Applies to midsize SUVs with LED headlamps, model years 2020-2022. Headlamps may flicker at idle while charging voltage is normal and no battery warning appears. Check the lamp driver module for stored codes. Repair: update the lamp driver module software.

messages.content: At stoplights at night the headlights and dash lights pulse dim and bright, and the battery warning light flickers, even on warm evenings. It's fine once I'm moving. My compact sedan is a 2013 with the 1.8-liter engine and 96k on the clock. What would you look at first?

snippets.title: Low-speed pulsation felt in the seat from rear drums

snippets.title: Pressure cap test
snippets.text: Applies to all engines. Fit the radiator or reservoir cap to a cap adapter on the pressure tester and pump until the cap vents. It should hold at least its stamped rating. snippets.title: Front clunk from loose subframe bolts

snippets.title: Slow cranking on a hot engine
snippets.text: Applies to all vehicles. If the engine turns over noticeably slower when hot than when cold, measure starter current draw with an inductive clamp while cranking with fuel disabled. snippets.title: Hot restart delay from fuel pump relay contacts
snippets.text: Applies to 5.5L V8 engines, model years 2021-2023. After towing or extended idling in hot weather, worn contacts in the fuel pump relay can delay fuel pump prime on restart. snippets.title: Radiator temperature drop check
snippets.text: Applies to all engines. With the engine at operating temperature and the thermostat open, use an infrared thermometer to compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical. A much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow through the radiator.

snippets.title: Electric radiator fan operation check
snippets.text: Applies to vehicles with electric radiator fans (2.0L I4, 2.4L I4, 2.5L I4, 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 1.4L turbo I4, 3.5L V6 and 3.4L V6 engines; not the 5.5L V8). With the engine at operating temperature and idling, turn the AC on or command the radiator fan on with a scan tool. The fan should start within a few moments. A fan that does not run lets coolant temperature climb in traffic while highway airflow keeps it normal at speed.

snippets.title: Coolant level and trapped air check
snippets.text: Applies to all engines. With the engine cold, remove the radiator cap or degas bottle cap and check that coolant is at the neck or the cold-fill line. Low coolant, or air trapped near the thermostat housing, causes temperature to swing upward at idle while airflow at speed can mask it.

messages.content: I have a 2019 compact sedan with the 2.0L four-cylinder, about 152,437 miles. The temperature gauge climbs toward hot when I'm sitting in traffic or at a long light, and it drops back to normal as soon as I'm moving at highway speed. Where do I start?
With the engine cold, open the radiator or degas bottle cap and look at whether coolant is right up to the neck or the cold-fill line [SM-4631]. That result will show whether this area is involved.

OK, that checks out. With the engine warm and idling, turn the AC on or command the radiator fan on with a scan tool and confirm the fan starts [SM-8812].

snippets.title: Cranking compression test

Drop should be under 0.3 V on the positive side and under 0.2 V on the ground side.
